extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, media scholars, and students of journalism/media criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and explanatory principles for how newspapers gather, select, shape, and present news, and for how readers and institutions judge newspaper quality and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader loyalty determines newspaper independence
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper that can really depend upon the loyalty of its readers is as independent as a newspaper can be, given the economics of modern journalism. 'More readers, more independence of the influence of advertisers; fewer readers and more dependence on the advertiser.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A body of readers who stay by it through thick and thin is a power greater than any individual advertiser. If a paper betrays its readers for an advertiser, the publisher either shares the advertiser's views or doubts his readers' support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic base and advertiser clientele shape content
rubrics_metrics.description: Roughly speaking, the economic support for general news gathering is in the price paid for advertised goods by the fairly prosperous sections of cities... These buying publics are the clientele among whom it pays best to advertise in a newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because advertisers target prosperous urban consumers, newspapers tailor content to attract and hold those customers; publishers themselves are usually members of these urban communities and see the world through their associates' lenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers are judged by treatment of matters within readers' experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of us tends to judge a newspaper, if we judge it at all, by its treatment of that part of the news in which we feel ourselves involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers most strictly hold a paper accountable on local or personally relevant items (business, church, party); accurate or satisfactory handling of those items secures immunity from strong criticism by those readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal constraints limit remedies for general readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The general reader of a newspaper has no standing in law if he thinks he is being misled by the news. It is only the aggrieved party who can sue for slander or libel, and he has to prove a material injury to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law embodies the tradition that general news is not a matter of common concern except as to matters vaguely described as immoral or seditious; this legal reality affects the incentives and accountability of newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: News requires overt acts or objectified form to be reportable
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a series of events become news they have usually to make themselves noticeable in some more or less overt act... There must be a manifestation. The course of events must assume a certain definable shape, and until it is in a phase where some aspect is an accomplished fact, news does not separate itself from the ocean of possible truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of manifest forms: bankruptcy filings, fires, collisions, arrests, the introduction of a bill, speeches, votes, meetings, published editorials, sales, price changes—these create the fixable points reporters use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and quality of record systems determine news certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a very direct relation between the certainty of news and the system of record. Where there is a good machinery of record (stock exchange, election returns, births/deaths) the news service works with great precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When official records or reliable tickers exist, coverage is precise and timely; where record systems are weak or absent, news becomes speculative, debatable, or neglected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects lacking objective records are debated or neglected
rubrics_metrics.description: All news about states of mind... descriptions of personalities, of sincerity, aspiration, motive, intention, of mass feeling, of national feeling, the policies of foreign governments... involve data that are at best spasmodically recorded. Then the news on these subjects is bound to be debatable, when it is not wholly neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex social conditions (working conditions, wages, efficiency of labor, unemployment, discrimination) require investigation and are rarely covered adequately by routine daily reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agents/publicity men filter and shape what becomes news
rubrics_metrics.description: Information for the public is first filtered through publicity agents. The publicity man stands between the group and the newspapers; he is censor and propagandist, responsible only to his employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because facts often lack an obvious shape, organizations hire press agents to package and present situations in a form journalists can use; press agents may stage stunts to create newsworthy events.

rubrics_metrics.name: News value often depends on stunts or overt actions arranged by PR
rubrics_metrics.description: The good press agent understands that the virtues of his cause are not news unless they are such strange virtues that they jut right out of the routine of life... If the publicity man wishes free publicity he has to start something. He arranges a stunt... The suffragists knew this... and kept suffrage in the news by acting on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organized groups seeking attention must produce visible events (demonstrations, protests, stunts) to make their issues salient to daily news routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers supplement general news with other features to hold readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper takes to itself a variety of other features, all primarily designed to hold a body of readers... They go to the dazzling levels of society, to scandal and crime, to sports, pictures, actresses, advice to the lovelorn, high-school notes, women's pages, buyer's pages, cooking receipts, comics, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because political and major-event interest is intermittent, papers use lifestyle, entertainment, and partisan features to differentiate themselves and maintain steady circulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting quality constrained by pay, status, and resource allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting... is the most poorly paid branch of newspaper work, and is the least regarded. By and large, able men go into it only by necessity or for experience, with the intention of being graduated as soon as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative or in-depth reporting requires time, money, and special talent; daily papers rarely can sustain lengthy investigations (Pittsburgh Surveys example), so routine reporting predominates.

rubrics_metrics.name: News is a stylized account, not a mirror of complex realities
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first instance, therefore, the news is not a mirror of social conditions, but the report of an aspect that has obtruded itself... The news is an account of the overt phases that are interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters translate complex, often unseen processes into stereotyped, simplified accounts that readers can map onto their own experience; this stylization can misrepresent deeper causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage tends to focus on how events affect readers' immediate lives
rubrics_metrics.description: The easiest way is to let the news be uncovered by the overt act, and to describe the event as the story of interference with the reader's life. That is where his attention is first aroused, and his interest most easily enlisted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local impact and convenience/inconvenience are often the primary lenses through which events (e.g., strikes) are presented, rather than the underlying issues important to affected parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter skill and experience influence ability to 'uncover' news
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturally there is room for wide difference of opinion as to when events have a shape that can be reported. A good journalist will find news oftener than a hack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some reporters can anticipate or perceive emerging news (detecting danger in a listing building, guessing appointments); training and habit of seeing are important to find stories before they become obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization of news via metropolitan dailies and press associations
rubrics_metrics.description: About one hundred and seventy-five printed in cities having over one hundred thousand inhabitants constitute the press for 'general news.' They make up the great press associations which cooperate in the exchange of news... the rural press and the special press by and large, take their general news from these key papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A relatively small number of metropolitan newspapers and news services set the agenda for national and international reporting; this centralization affects diversity and reliance across the press.
